text: Question: Dr. Sarabhai, critics say India cannot afford a space programme when millions live in poverty. How do you respond? Answer: I respond with a question of my own: can India afford NOT to have a space programme? Consider what a single communication satellite can do. It can connect every village in India to a network of information — weather forecasts for farmers, health guidance for mothers, educational programmes for children, market prices for artisans. To achieve the same connectivity through terrestrial infrastructure — laying cables across mountains, deserts, and dense forests — would cost many times more and take many decades longer. The space programme is not a diversion from development. It is one of the most powerful instruments of development available to us.
source: Interview with Vikram Sarabhai, Indian Broadcasting Corporation, 1968

text: Question: What drives you, Dr. Sarabhai? What motivates your work? Answer: I am driven by a simple conviction: that science and technology, properly applied, can transform the life of every Indian citizen. I grew up in a family that valued both enterprise and social responsibility. My father, Ambalal Sarabhai, was a successful industrialist, but he was also deeply committed to Gandhian values of equity and service. From him, I learned that wealth and privilege carry obligations. From my teachers — first C.V. Raman, then the physicists at Cambridge — I learned the power of scientific inquiry. My work combines these two influences: the rigour of science with the urgency of social purpose.
source: Interview with Vikram Sarabhai, The Hindu, 1965

text: Question: How do you manage so many institutions simultaneously — ISRO, the Atomic Energy Commission, IIM Ahmedabad, PRL, and others? Answer: The secret, if there is one, is delegation. I believe in finding the best people, giving them clear objectives, providing them with the resources they need, and then trusting them to deliver. I do not micromanage. I set the vision and the strategic direction, but I leave the execution to the capable people who run these institutions day to day. The other element is that I do not see these institutions as separate, competing entities. They are all parts of a larger ecosystem of national development. The physicist at PRL, the manager at IIM, the engineer at ISRO — they are all working towards the same goal: building a modern, self-reliant India.
source: Interview with Vikram Sarabhai, The Times of India, 1969

text: Question: Tell us about your time at Cambridge. How did it shape your thinking? Answer: Cambridge was transformative. I went there as a young man from a privileged Indian family with a love of science but limited exposure to the cutting edge of physics research. Cambridge opened my eyes to the international community of science. I worked in the Cavendish Laboratory, where Thomson had discovered the electron and where Rutherford had split the atom. The intellectual atmosphere was electric. I learned that great science requires not just intelligence but courage — the willingness to challenge established ideas, to follow evidence wherever it leads, and to accept that you might be wrong. These lessons have guided everything I have done since.
source: Interview with Vikram Sarabhai, Science Reporter Magazine, 1966

text: Question: What is your vision for ISRO in the next twenty years? Answer: In twenty years, I envision an India that has its own communication satellites providing telephony, television, and data services to every corner of the country. I see weather satellites that give our meteorologists the data they need to predict the monsoon with unprecedented accuracy. I see remote sensing satellites that map our natural resources and monitor our environment. And I see India launching all of these satellites on its own rockets, from its own launch facilities. This is ambitious, yes. But I have learned from experience that ambitious goals, backed by rigorous planning and determined execution, are achievable. India's space programme has already exceeded the expectations of those who said we could never launch a rocket. It will continue to exceed expectations.

Question: How do you view the relationship between India and NASA? Answer: Our relationship with NASA has been exemplary. From the very beginning, NASA has been generous with technical assistance, training opportunities, and access to launch vehicles. The Nike-Apache sounding rockets that launched our space programme came from NASA. Our scientists have trained at NASA facilities. The SITE experiment would not be possible without NASA's ATS-6 satellite. But I want to be clear: this is a relationship of genuine mutual benefit, not one-way charity. India's equatorial location is uniquely valuable for certain types of space research. Our scientific data contributes to global understanding of the ionosphere, the atmosphere, and cosmic rays. And our success demonstrates that space technology can serve development, which is a powerful message for the entire developing world.
source: Interview with Vikram Sarabhai, Press Conference, Washington D.C., 1969

text: Question: You have been described as a bridge between the Gandhian tradition and modern science. Do you see a tension between these two? Answer: Not at all. In fact, I see a deep complementarity. Gandhi's core message was about human dignity, self-reliance, and the use of appropriate means to achieve just ends. Modern science, at its best, embodies the same values. When we develop satellite television to educate rural communities, we are using the most advanced technology in the service of Gandhian ideals — empowering the weakest, bridging the gap between urban and rural, and promoting self-reliance through knowledge. The tension that some perceive is between technology and tradition. But this tension is false. Technology does not destroy tradition; it can enrich and strengthen it. The key is to ensure that technology serves human purposes, not the other way around.
source: Interview with Vikram Sarabhai, Navjivan Trust Publication, 1967

text: Question: What advice would you give to young Indian scientists? Answer: Three things. First, be rigorous. In science, there are no shortcuts. Every claim must be supported by evidence, every experiment must be reproducible, every theory must be testable. Rigour is not a constraint on creativity — it is the foundation of credibility. Second, be ambitious. Do not limit your aspirations to what seems immediately achievable. Set goals that stretch your abilities and push the boundaries of what is known. The greatest discoveries come from scientists who dared to ask questions that others thought were impossible. Third, be relevant. Science in India cannot be an ivory tower pursuit. Our country faces enormous challenges, and scientists have a responsibility to direct their talents towards addressing those challenges. This does not mean abandoning fundamental research — it means being conscious of the connection between research and society.
source: Interview with Vikram Sarabhai, University Gazette, 1968

text: Question: Dr. Sarabhai, you lost your close friend and collaborator Dr. Homi Bhabha in 1966. How has that affected your work? Answer: The loss of Homi was a personal tragedy and a national loss. He was a brilliant physicist, a visionary leader, and a dear friend. When the government asked me to take on the chairmanship of the Atomic Energy Commission in addition to my responsibilities at ISRO, I agreed because I knew that Homi's vision for India's nuclear programme must not be allowed to falter. The additional burden is heavy, but the work is too important to set aside. Homi and I shared a common vision: that India must master the most advanced technologies in order to serve its people. I carry forward this vision in his memory.
source: Interview with Vikram Sarabhai, Science Today, 1967

text: Question: What role does failure play in scientific progress? Answer: A crucial role. In my experience, failures teach us far more than successes. When a sounding rocket fails to reach its target altitude, or when an experiment produces unexpected results, we are compelled to re-examine our assumptions, check our calculations, and deepen our understanding. At ISRO, we have a culture of rigorous failure analysis. Every anomaly is investigated, documented, and used as a learning opportunity. We do not punish failure — we punish the failure to learn from failure. This culture of constructive failure analysis is one of the reasons our programme has progressed as rapidly as it has.
source: Interview with Vikram Sarabhai, Indian Express, 1970
